Fuel-Optimized Route Planning API

A Django REST backend that plans cost-optimal fuel stops along a route using graph-based shortest-path search and spatial indexing.

Backend DeveloperSpotter Labs — prototypeFeb 2026

Overview

A backend prototype for trip fuel planning: given a route and a vehicle's range and MPG, it recommends the fuel stops that minimize total trip fuel cost.

Problem

Picking cost-efficient fuel stops along a long route isn't a simple nearest-station lookup — it has to account for the vehicle's range and MPG and the total cost across the whole trip, without exhaustively checking every station along the way.

Solution

I modeled the route as a graph and used a Dijkstra-based shortest-path algorithm to find the minimum-cost sequence of fuel stops within the vehicle's range. Fuel-station retrieval uses H3 spatial indexing with bounding-box filtering to keep candidate lookups fast, and the API returns route polylines, per-mile fuel spend, and stop recommendations from a single call, built on a caching-ready architecture with PostgreSQL/PostGIS-ready data modeling and Redis.

My role

I designed and built the backend end-to-end: the Clean Architecture REST API, the Dijkstra-based optimization engine, the H3 spatial indexing layer, and the caching-ready data layer.

Engineering challenges

Modeling fuel stops as a shortest-path problem

Minimizing total trip cost isn't the same as minimizing distance or number of stops. Representing candidate fuel stations and route segments as a graph let a standard Dijkstra search do the actual optimization, instead of hand-rolling heuristics.

Keeping station lookups fast along a long route

Checking every fuel station against every route segment doesn't scale. H3 spatial indexing combined with bounding-box filtering narrows the candidate set before the optimization step ever runs, which is what keeps route computation fast.

Technical decisions

Clean Architecture on Django REST Framework

For a backend meant to be handed off or extended, keeping the domain logic (the optimization engine) separate from the framework and infrastructure layers made the code testable independent of Django itself.

H3 over naive geo-radius queries

A naive radius query against every station gets slower as the station dataset grows. H3's hexagonal indexing gives constant-ish lookup behavior that scales better with data size.

Results

  • Delivered a working single-call routing flow: route polyline, per-mile fuel spend, and fuel-stop recommendations in one response.
  • Reduced fuel-station query complexity via H3 spatial indexing and bounding-box filtering.
